exercises.prompt:
`i` is `PIC S99`. How many lines does this loop display?

```cobol
    PERFORM VARYING i FROM 10 BY -3 UNTIL i < 1
        DISPLAY i
    END-PERFORM
```

feedback.message: Not yet: the condition is tested before each pass. Is `1 < 1` true?
Not yet: after 1 comes −2, and `−2 < 1` stops the loop before it is displayed.

hints: The loop stops as soon as `i < 1` is true, before running the body.
exercises.solution: `i` takes 10, 7, 4 and 1; each passes the test and is displayed (as `+10`, `+07`, `+04`, `+01`). The next value, −2, satisfies `i < 1`, so the loop ends: **4** lines. `i` must be signed here; with an unsigned `PIC 99`, −2 would be stored as 2 and the loop would never end.

exercises.prompt:
`score` is 85. What does this print?

```cobol
    EVALUATE TRUE
        WHEN score >= 50 DISPLAY "pass"
        WHEN score >= 80 DISPLAY "distinction"
        WHEN OTHER DISPLAY "fail"
    END-EVALUATE
```

feedback.message: Not yet: `EVALUATE` runs the first `WHEN` that is true and then stops.
Not yet: `EVALUATE` never falls through to later `WHEN`s.

hints: Which `WHEN` is tested first, and is it true for 85?
exercises.solution: The `WHEN`s are tried in order and only the first true one runs. 85 ≥ 50, so the program prints **`pass`**. To get `distinction`, put the stricter test first.

exercises.prompt:
`balance` is −5. Which lines does this print? List them separated by commas.

```cobol
    IF balance < 0
        DISPLAY "overdrawn".
        DISPLAY "fee charged"
    DISPLAY "done"
    STOP RUN.
```
hints: Every `DISPLAY` after the full stop runs whatever the balance.
exercises.solution: The `IF` ends at the full stop, so it controls only `DISPLAY "overdrawn"`. Since −5 < 0, that line prints, and the other two `DISPLAY`s run unconditionally: **overdrawn, fee charged, done**. For a positive balance the program would still print `fee charged`, which is the bug.

exercises.prompt:
`k` is `PIC 9 VALUE 5` and `say-it` is a paragraph that displays `k`. How many lines are printed?

```cobol
    PERFORM say-it 3 TIMES
    PERFORM say-it UNTIL k > 4
    PERFORM say-it WITH TEST AFTER UNTIL k > 4
```

feedback.message: Not yet: the plain `UNTIL` tests before the first pass, and `5 > 4` is already true.
Not yet: `WITH TEST AFTER` always runs the body at least once.

hints: Nothing changes `k`, so `k > 4` is always true.
Which of the two `UNTIL` loops tests before running?
exercises.solution: `3 TIMES` gives three lines. `UNTIL k > 4` tests first and finds it true, so it runs zero times. `WITH TEST AFTER` runs once and then finds the condition true. 3 + 0 + 1 = **4**.

exercises.prompt:
How many lines does this complete procedure division print?

```cobol
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
main-para.
    PERFORM greet
    DISPLAY "main done".
greet.
    DISPLAY "hello".
```

feedback.message: Not yet: what happens when `main-para` reaches its end? There is no `STOP RUN`.

hints: After `main-para` finishes, where does control go?
exercises.solution: `PERFORM greet` prints `hello`, then `main done` is printed. With no `STOP RUN`, control falls through into the next paragraph, `greet`, which prints `hello` again before the program reaches its end: **3** lines.

options.label: `IF region-code = "N" OR region-code = "S"`
options.feedback: Yes. This is an abbreviated combined condition: the subject and operator carry over to each following value.

options.label: `IF (region-code = "N") OR ("S" is true)`, which is always true
options.feedback: Not yet. That is how C or Python would read a similar expression, but COBOL expands the abbreviation.

options.label: `IF region-code = "NS"`
options.feedback: Not yet. `OR` does not join literals together.

options.label: It is a syntax error.
options.feedback: Not yet. It is valid and very common COBOL.

hints: COBOL lets you omit the repeated subject and relation.
exercises.solution: COBOL expands it to **`region-code = "N" OR region-code = "S"`**. A clearer alternative is an 88 level, `88 north-or-south VALUE "N" "S"`, tested with `IF north-or-south`.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are good reasons for modern COBOL style (scope terminators such as `END-IF`, and one full stop at the end of each paragraph)? Choose all that apply.

options.label: A full stop ends every open conditional statement, so a stray one can silently move statements out of an `IF`.
options.feedback: Yes. The compiler cannot warn, because the result is legal.

options.label: Inline `PERFORM ... END-PERFORM` and nested `IF`s inside loops need scope terminators to be written at all.
options.feedback: Yes. A full stop inside an inline `PERFORM` ends the sentence before `END-PERFORM` is reached, and GnuCOBOL rejects it with `PERFORM statement not terminated by END-PERFORM`; an `IF` inside the loop must be closed with `END-IF`.

options.label: Full stops make programs run more slowly.
options.feedback: Not yet. Punctuation has no effect on run-time speed; the reasons are about meaning and safety.

options.label: Indentation alone shows a reader where each block ends.
options.feedback: Not yet. Indentation means nothing to the compiler; the stray-period example was perfectly indented and still wrong.

hints: Think about what the compiler uses to decide where an `IF` ends.
exercises.solution: **a** and **b**. The full stop is a powerful terminator: it closes every open scope at once. Scope terminators close exactly one, so blocks can nest safely, and edits cannot change the structure by accident. Indentation is for people only.
